title: The parables, looking back
hookLine: a sower, a lost coin, a mustard seed: stories that still work on you
tomorrow: what do you do with news you can't explain yet?

lines: A QUESTION, ANSWERED WITH A STORY.
A SOWER, A COIN, A SEED.
cards: Ask a yes-or-no question and get a story about a farmer back. It can feel like help, or like a dodge. Jesus answered this way all the time: a sower, a woman sweeping for one lost coin, a mustard seed.
So were the parables meant to make things plain, or to keep them hidden? Christians have read them both ways, and each side has a verse.

teach.h: VIEW ONE: AS THEY WERE ABLE.
teach.b: View one: the stories are a kindness. Mark says, “And with many such parables spake he the word unto them, as they were able to hear it.” As they were able.
A parable meets a listener where they are: farmers hear about seed, a woman with ten coins hears about the one she lost. Nobody needs training to follow it.
View two: the stories also sift.

teach.h: BOTH: HE EXPLAINED TO THOSE WHO ASKED.
teach.b: When his friends ask why he talks this way, Jesus says that for those outside, everything comes in parables, “That seeing they may see, and not perceive.” He's echoing the prophet Isaiah.

On this reading a parable never forces itself on anyone; it waits for whoever wants it enough to ask. Both sides have a fair case. The first can point to Mark's note that the common people heard him gladly.
The second can point to how often even his friends were lost. And here's the detail both keep, worth telling a friend tonight: the explanation went to whoever came back.
Mark says, “when they were alone, he expounded all things to his disciples.” The sower is a story about this very thing.
The same seed falls on four kinds of ground, and Jesus ends, “He that hath ears to hear, let him hear.”
Looking back from near the top, a parable heard long ago may say something new now. The seed didn't change. The ground did.

how: Christians hear the parables read in worship, study them in groups, and return to them over a lifetime; some find a different detail stands out each time.

o: short stories of Jesus that keep on teaching
sayings of the prophets set to music
fables that each end with a stated moral

p: same seed, four kinds of ground

s: a parable always ends by stating its one moral
the sower ends: he that hath ears to hear, let him hear. the hearing is left to the listener.
Mark's line 'seeing they may see, and not perceive' echoes the prophet Isaiah
Jesus answers his friends with words from Isaiah.
in the sower story, the seed changes from field to field
the seed is the same every time; the ground is what differs.

games.q: a friend says, "parables are just Jesus being clear with simple stories." give the best case for the other view.
o: parables were only meant for children; adults got plain teaching.
in Mark, Jesus says parables let some see and not perceive; they wait for those who ask.
Jesus spoke in riddles so that nobody could ever understand him.
games.why: Mark 4 holds both: 'as they were able to hear it', and 'seeing they may see, and not perceive'. both views agree the explanation went to those who came back.

practice: Choose the parable that has stayed with you longest, and tell it out loud in your own words, start to finish, slowly. Notice which part catches now; it may not be the part that caught at first.
If you pray, ask what it's still saying.

wordCard.voice: The parables. The short stories Jesus told, a sower, a coin, a seed, plain to some, waiting for others, and heard anew as the listener changes.

orig.note: the Greek word for 'parable', as in Mark 4:33: something set alongside.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: stories still working, and the meaning goes to whoever comes back and asks. Until tomorrow.
